label: The timing graph
lesson:
# The timing graph

A static timer never simulates a circuit. It turns the netlist into a directed graph and propagates numbers along it. Every later idea in timing analysis, arrival times, required times, slack, incremental updates, path enumeration, is an operation on this graph. Its shape decides what the timer can compute in one pass and what it must approximate, so a tool designer has to know exactly which pieces of the netlist become nodes and edges.

## Pins as nodes, arcs as edges

Each node is a pin of a cell instance or a top-level port. Edges come in two kinds. A cell arc joins an input pin to an output pin of one instance; its delay and output slew come from that cell's Liberty timing arc, evaluated at the input slew and output load. A net arc joins a net's driver pin to one of its sink pins; its delay comes from the wire's parasitics. Paths begin at startpoints, the input ports and the clock pins of sequential cells, where a clock-to-Q arc launches data. They end at endpoints, the data pins of flip-flops and latches and the output ports. A flip-flop has no propagation arc from D to Q: D carries a setup and hold check against the clock pin, and Q is launched from the clock. Sequential cells therefore cut the graph into combinational pieces.

## Counting cell arcs and net arcs

The graph's size is easy to compute, and it is linear in the netlist. A single-output combinational cell with $k$ inputs contributes $k$ cell arcs, one per input pin. A net with $f$ sinks contributes $f$ net arcs. Take a NAND2 driving three pins, an AOI21 driving two and an inverter driving four. The cells add $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$ cell arcs and the nets add $3 + 2 + 4 = 9$ net arcs, 15 edges in all. Real timers also store separate rise and fall data on each arc and may split one Liberty arc by timing sense, but the count of graph edges still grows with pins, not with paths. That is the property that makes a full-chip timer possible: a design with billions of paths has only millions of arcs.

## Loops, disabled arcs and why a DAG matters

Propagation visits nodes in topological order, so every fanin is final before its fanout is evaluated, and the whole graph is timed in time proportional to its arcs. That needs a directed acyclic graph. Flip-flops already break the sequential feedback loops. A combinational loop, two cross-coupled NAND gates for instance, would make arrival times depend on themselves, so the timer breaks it by disabling one arc and warns. Designers can also remove arcs deliberately with set_disable_timing, for example through a mode-control pin. Every disabled arc deletes paths from the reports, so disabled arcs are reviewed as carefully as timing exceptions. Rise and fall are tracked separately at every node, because the two transitions have different delays and an inverting arc maps one to the other.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapters 1 and 7; the OpenSTA source, whose Graph and Levelize classes build and order this graph.

A) The D pin of a flip-flop

B) An output port

C) The clock pin of a flip-flop

D) The output pin of an inverter in the middle of a path

problems.e: Paths start at input ports and at sequential clock pins, where the clock-to-Q arc launches data. D pins and output ports are endpoints.

C) Flip-flops have no Liberty data

D) Q always has zero delay

problems.q:
A netlist contains a combinational loop through two NAND gates. What must the timer do before propagating arrivals?

A) Report an infinite arrival time at every pin

B) Treat the loop as a multicycle path

C) Iterate arrival times until they converge

D) Break the loop by disabling one arc so the graph is acyclic
problems.a: Break the loop by disabling one arc so the graph is acyclic
problems.e: Propagation in topological order needs a DAG. Timers break combinational loops by disabling an arc and warn about it.

problems.q:
A designer marks an arc with set_disable_timing. What happens to the timing graph?

A) The cell is removed from the netlist

B) The arc's delay becomes zero

C) That arc is removed, so no path propagates through it

D) The arc becomes a false path only for hold
problems.a: That arc is removed, so no path propagates through it
problems.e: Disabling an arc deletes it from propagation. Paths that relied on it disappear from reports, which is why disabled arcs must be audited.

problems.q:
How does the size of the timing graph grow with the netlist?

A) With the number of clock domains only

B) Quadratically in the number of cells

C) Exponentially in the number of paths

D) Linearly in the number of pins and arcs
problems.a: Linearly in the number of pins and arcs
problems.e: The graph holds one node per pin and one edge per arc. It is the number of paths, not the graph, that grows exponentially.

label: Timing sense and unateness of arcs
lesson:
# Timing sense and unateness of arcs

A timer does not propagate one arrival time per pin but two, one for a rising and one for a falling transition. Which input transition produces which output transition depends on the cell's logic function, captured in Liberty as each arc's timing sense. Getting this mapping right is what lets the timer pair the correct delay table with the correct transition, and it explains why some cells, such as XOR, make timing more pessimistic than others.

## Positive, negative and non-unate arcs

An arc is positive unate when a rising input can only cause a rising output and a falling input only a falling output. Buffers, AND and OR gates are positive unate from each input. An arc is negative unate when the output moves the opposite way: inverters, NAND, NOR, AOI and OAI gates. Static CMOS gates are naturally negative unate, because a rising input turns on an NMOS pull-down. An arc is non-unate when the output direction depends on the other inputs. In an XOR, a rising input A makes the output rise if B is 0 and fall if B is 1. Liberty records this in the arc's timing_sense attribute as positive_unate, negative_unate or non_unate, and the timer reads it when it builds the graph.

## Following a transition through a chain

To know which transition reaches the end of a path, walk the arcs in order. A positive-unate arc keeps the direction, a negative-unate arc flips it. A falling input through an OR, a buffer and a NOR becomes falling, falling, then rising: the path ends with a rising transition. A timer does this for both transitions at once. It keeps a rise arrival and a fall arrival at each pin, and a negative-unate arc maps the input rise arrival plus the cell_fall delay to the output fall arrival, and the input fall arrival plus the cell_rise delay to the output rise arrival. Path reports show the direction at each pin with a rise or fall marker, which is how an engineer checks that the right delay tables were used.

## Non-unate arcs propagate both edges

Through a non-unate arc either output transition is possible, so the timer must propagate both: the output rise arrival is the worse of the input rise and fall arrivals plus the rise delay, and likewise for fall. Once both directions exist they continue downstream, even through later unate arcs, because a buffer passes a rise as a rise and a fall as a fall. For example, a falling edge into an XOR, then a NAND, then an AND yields both a rise and a fall at the end. This is a source of pessimism: the timer combines the worst of two transitions that may not both be reachable from one real input vector. Mode-specific constants (set_case_analysis) can resolve a non-unate arc to a unate one when a side input is known.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 3 on timing arcs and unateness; the Liberty reference manual on timing_sense.

label: Levelizing the timing graph
lesson:
# Levelizing the timing graph

Before a timer propagates anything it levelizes the graph: it assigns every node a level so that each arc goes from a lower level to a higher one. Levels are a topological order with extra structure. They let the timer process the graph as a sequence of independent batches, schedule incremental updates, and run nodes of one level in parallel. OpenSTA's search is built around this levelized order.

## The level of a node

Sources, the startpoints with no fanin, sit at level 0. Every other node's level is one more than the largest level among its fanins: $\ell(v) = 1 + \max_{u \to v} \ell(u)$. Compute it in any topological order. For the arcs $A \to B$, $A \to C$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, node $A$ is level 0, $B$ is level 1, $C$ is level 2 because its deepest fanin $B$ is at level 1, and $D$ is level 3. Note that $C$ is not at level 1 even though it has a fanin at level 0; the maximum governs. This guarantees that when the timer reaches level $k$, every fanin of every node at that level is already final.

## Depth is the longest path in arcs

The largest level in the graph is its depth: the number of arcs on the longest path from any source, counting arcs rather than delays. It is exactly the longest-path problem on a DAG with unit weights, solved by the same one-pass recurrence. Depth tells a tool designer how many sequential steps a levelized propagation needs, even with unlimited parallel workers. A wide, shallow graph parallelizes well; a deep chain of carry logic does not. Logic depth also reappears in timing itself: advanced on-chip variation tables index their derates by the number of cells on a path. For the four-node example above, the depth is 3.

## Levels as batches of independent work

Nodes on the same level never feed each other, since an arc always climbs at least one level. A timer can therefore evaluate all nodes of one level in parallel, then move to the next, and the number of nodes on a level measures the parallelism available there. Levels also organize incremental timing: when an arc changes, the timer queues the affected nodes by level and processes them in increasing order, so no node is evaluated before its fanins settle and none is evaluated twice. OpenSTA keeps the levels up to date as the netlist changes, relevelizing only the region that moved, because a full relevelization after every edit would waste the savings of incremental analysis.

## Going deeper

Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms", the chapter on topological sort and DAG shortest paths; the OpenSTA source, Levelize and BfsIterator.

label: Forward propagation of arrival times
prereqs: Timing sense and unateness of arcs
lesson:
# Forward propagation of arrival times

The arrival time at a pin is when the signal there settles, measured from the launching clock edge. Block-based static timing computes it for every pin in one forward pass over the timing graph, with a maximum at every merge. This is the core numerical kernel of a timer: it must be exact, fast and incremental, and everything else, required times, slack and optimization, is built on top of it.

## The max-plus recurrence

A startpoint gets its arrival from the clock: a flip-flop's Q pin arrives at the clock arrival plus clock-to-Q, and an input port at its input delay. Every other pin takes the latest of its fanins: $AT(v) = \max_{u \to v} \big(AT(u) + d(u,v)\big)$. The maximum is the right operator for setup, because a gate's output is not settled until its last input has settled. Take a source $S$ at 5 ps with arcs $S \to A$ (17 ps), $S \to B$ (16 ps) and $A \to B$ (8 ps). Then $AT(A) = 22$ ps, and $B$ sees $5 + 16 = 21$ and $22 + 8 = 30$, so $AT(B) = 30$ ps. The arrival is a property of the pin, not of one path, which is why the recurrence touches each arc once.

## Propagating to the endpoints

Visit the nodes in topological or level order, so that every fanin is final first, and apply the recurrence at each node. The latest arrival at an endpoint is then the delay of the longest path into it, found without listing a single path. This is longest path in a DAG, which is easy even though longest path in a general graph is hard. The cost is linear in the number of arcs. For a chain with a side branch, $S$ at 0 ps, $S \to A$ 20 ps, $A \to C$ 15 ps, $S \to C$ 30 ps and $C \to E$ 10 ps, the arrivals are $A = 20$, $C = \max(35, 30) = 35$ and $E = 45$ ps. A real timer stores this per transition (rise and fall) and per clock domain, but the recurrence is the same.

## Early arrivals for hold

Hold checks ask the opposite question: how soon can new data arrive? The same pass with a minimum computes the earliest arrival, $AT_{min}(v) = \min_{u \to v} \big(AT_{min}(u) + d_{min}(u,v)\big)$, using minimum delays from the fast corner or early derates. In the example above the earliest arrival at $C$ is $\min(35, 30) = 30$ ps, so $E$ is at 40 ps early and 45 ps late. Timers propagate both values together in one traversal, storing a min and a max arrival per pin and transition. Using a max where a min is needed would make hold analysis optimistic, which is the most dangerous kind of error in a timer: it reports a passing check on silicon that fails.

## Going deeper

Sapatnekar, "Timing" (2004), chapter on static timing analysis; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 7.

label: Arrival and required times
lesson:
# Arrival and required times

Arrival times say when data settles; required times say when it must settle. A timer computes the first forward from the startpoints and the second backward from the endpoints, and their difference is slack. The backward pass mirrors the forward one, with a minimum instead of a maximum, and it is what turns a single endpoint constraint into a deadline at every internal pin, the deadline an optimizer reads when it decides which gate to resize.

## Required time at an endpoint

At a flip-flop's data pin, setup requires the data to settle a setup time before the capturing clock edge reaches the flop. With period $T$, capture clock latency $L_{cap}$ and setup time $t_{su}$, the required time is $RAT = T + L_{cap} - t_{su}$, measured from the launching source edge at 0. For a 1000 ps clock, a capture latency of 60 ps and a 40 ps setup, the data must arrive by $1000 + 60 - 40 = 1020$ ps. At an output port, the required time is the capturing edge minus the output delay from the SDC. With ideal clocks the latency term is zero, and the endpoint required time is simply $T - t_{su}$. Uncertainty, when present, is subtracted as well.

## Backward propagation with a minimum

For an internal pin $u$, every fanout arc $u \to v$ imposes a deadline: the signal must leave $u$ by $RAT(v) - d(u,v)$ to reach $v$ in time. All fanouts must be satisfied, so $RAT(u) = \min_{u \to v} \big(RAT(v) - d(u,v)\big)$. Visit nodes in reverse topological order. Suppose $u$ feeds endpoint $X$ through 20 ps with $RAT(X) = 150$ ps and endpoint $Y$ through 35 ps with $RAT(Y) = 120$ ps. The deadlines are 130 and 85 ps, so $RAT(u) = 85$ ps. One backward pass, linear in the arcs, gives every pin its deadline without listing paths.

## Why the minimum governs

The minimum is the mirror of the forward maximum. A pin can feed many endpoints, and the tightest one, the endpoint with the least room after its own path delay, sets the deadline for everything upstream. A startpoint deep in the graph inherits the strictest constraint among all endpoints it reaches. That is also why a single badly constrained endpoint, say an output delay set far too large, drags down the required times of every pin in its fanin cone and makes the optimizer chase phantom violations. For hold, the backward pass flips again: the hold requirement propagates with a maximum, since data must not arrive earlier than the latest hold deadline among the fanouts.

## Going deeper

Sapatnekar, "Timing" (2004), chapter on static timing analysis; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8.

label: What slack measures
lesson:
# What slack measures

Static timing analysis reduces a chip's timing to one signed number per endpoint: slack. Every optimization step downstream, gate sizing, buffering, placement moves, useful skew, reads slack and tries to raise its worst value. Knowing exactly what the number means, and what it does not, is the difference between fixing a timing problem and moving it somewhere else.

## Required minus arrival

The arrival time at an endpoint is the latest time its data input settles, found by propagating delays forward from the launching clock edge through the combinational logic. The required time is the latest moment the capturing flip-flop can accept that data: the next capturing clock edge, minus the flop's setup time, adjusted for clock skew and uncertainty. Setup slack is required time minus arrival time. A path with a 1000 ps clock, 940 ps of arrival and 40 ps of setup has slack $1000 - 40 - 940 = 20$ ps.

## The sign of slack

Positive slack is margin: the path could get that much slower and still meet timing. Negative slack is a violation, and its size says how much faster the path must become. Two summary numbers describe a whole design. Worst negative slack (WNS) is the most negative endpoint slack, the single worst path. Total negative slack (TNS) adds every negative endpoint slack, so it measures how widespread the problem is. A design with a WNS of -5 ps and a TNS of -3000 ps has a broad problem that local fixes cannot close.

## Hold slack runs the other way

Hold checks the opposite failure: new data arriving so early that it corrupts the value the capture flop is still holding from the previous cycle. Hold slack is the earliest arrival time minus the hold requirement, the same-edge clock arrival plus the hold time. Here a larger arrival time is better. That asymmetry is why timing fixes interact: upsizing a gate to speed a setup-critical path also speeds every short path through that gate, and can turn a passing hold check into a failing one.

problems.q:
Which expression defines setup slack at a flip-flop data pin?

B) Required time minus arrival time

problems.e: Slack is how much later the data could arrive and still be captured, which is required minus arrival.

label: Node slack and the critical path
lesson:
# Node slack and the critical path

Slack is defined at every pin, not only at endpoints. Once arrivals and required times are known everywhere, the slack of a pin is the slack of the worst path through it. That one number per pin is what lets an optimizer find critical regions without enumerating paths, and it gives a clean characterization of the critical path: the chain of pins that all share the worst slack.

## Slack at an endpoint

At an endpoint, setup slack is its required time minus its latest arrival, $S = RAT - AT$. Negative slack is a violation. With $RAT = 89$ ps and $AT = 99$ ps the endpoint fails by 10 ps. Each endpoint gets its own slack because it has its own clock, its own setup time and its own arrival. Endpoints of different clock domains or path groups are compared only through these slacks, never through raw arrival times, since the arrival time alone says nothing without the deadline it must meet. In a report, the endpoint list sorted by slack is the first thing a timing engineer reads.

## Slack at an internal node

At any pin $v$, $S(v) = RAT(v) - AT(v)$, where $AT$ came from the forward max pass and $RAT$ from the backward min pass. This equals the worst slack of any startpoint-to-endpoint path through $v$: the arrival is the latest path into $v$, and the required time is the tightest path out. Suppose a node has $AT = 35$ ps and $RAT = 50$ ps; every path through it has at least 15 ps of slack, and at least one path has exactly 15. Optimizers sort pins by this slack to decide where to work, because speeding up a pin with large slack cannot help the worst endpoint.

## The critical path shares one slack

Follow the worst path from its startpoint to its endpoint. Every pin on it has a slack equal to the endpoint's slack, because along that path the latest arrival and the tightest deadline come from the same path. So the critical path is exactly a chain of nodes whose slack equals the design's worst slack, and a timer can trace it by walking backward from the worst endpoint, at each step choosing the fanin that produced the arrival. When several paths tie, more nodes share the worst value. Counting nodes at the worst slack is a quick check: if a graph's worst slack is -10 ps and four nodes carry -10 ps, those four form the critical path or paths.

label: Worst and total negative slack
prereqs: Node slack and the critical path
lesson:
# Worst and total negative slack

A chip has millions of endpoints, each with a slack. Two summary numbers reduce them to something a team can track from run to run: worst negative slack and total negative slack. They answer different questions, and timing-driven tools optimize both. Misreading which one moved, or forgetting how positive slacks enter, leads to wrong conclusions about whether a change helped.

## Worst negative slack

WNS is the most negative endpoint slack in the design or path group: the single worst violation. If the endpoint slacks are -12, -3, 4 and 9 ps, WNS is -12 ps. It sets the minimum clock period the design reaches today: the period would have to grow by 12 ps for every endpoint to pass. Many reports clip it at zero, so a passing design shows a WNS of 0 rather than its smallest positive slack. WNS is fragile as an objective: an optimizer that fixes only the worst path can improve WNS by a few ps while hundreds of nearly-as-bad paths stay untouched, and the next run simply reports a different endpoint as the worst.

## Total negative slack

TNS sums the negative endpoint slacks; positive slacks contribute zero. For -12, -3, 4 and 9 ps, TNS is -15 ps. It measures how widespread the violations are. Two designs can share a WNS of -8 ps with TNS values of -9 ps and -4000 ps: the first has a local problem, the second a systematic one such as a bad floorplan or an over-tight constraint. TNS is a smoother objective than WNS because every failing endpoint contributes, so optimizers that improve many paths a little see progress. The number of failing endpoints is usually reported alongside it.

## How a fix changes TNS

When an ECO improves some endpoints, recompute TNS from the new slacks rather than adding the improvement directly. An endpoint that crosses zero contributes nothing, so it saves only what it was failing by. Suppose endpoints at -53, -7 and -27 ps each gain 15 ps. They become -38, $+8$ and -12 ps. The total improvement in TNS is $15 + 7 + 15 = 37$ ps, not $3 \times 15 = 45$ ps, because the endpoint at -7 ps could only give back 7. The same clipping explains why fixing a few large violations can move TNS more than many small fixes, and why a TNS target must always be read together with WNS and the failing-endpoint count.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8 on timing closure; the OpenSTA commands report_wns and report_tns.

label: Elmore delay of an RC tree
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Elmore delay of an RC tree

A routed net is not a wire with one delay. It is a tree: one driver, a trunk, branches and several sinks, each piece carrying resistance along its length and capacitance to ground. Timing analysis needs a delay number for every driver-to-sink arc of that tree, millions of times per run, so the formula must be cheap. The Elmore delay is that formula. It is the first estimate every timer computes and the baseline every better model is measured against.

## The first moment of the impulse response

Model the net as resistors in a tree, rooted at the driver, with a capacitor from every node to ground. Drive the root with an impulse and watch the voltage at a sink node $i$. Its response $h_i(t)$ rises and decays. W. C. Elmore proposed in 1948 that the delay to node $i$ be the mean of that response, its first moment $T_i = \int_0^\infty t\, h_i(t)\, dt$. For an RC tree the response is unimodal and the first moment upper-bounds the true 50% delay of a step input. That is why the estimate is safe to use in early optimization: it never claims a path is faster than it is.

## Shared resistance times downstream capacitance

The first moment has a closed form that needs no integration. For every capacitor $C_k$ in the tree, find the resistance that the path from the root to $k$ shares with the path from the root to the sink $i$. Call it $R_{ik}$. Then

$$T_i = \sum_k R_{ik} C_k.$$

Take a driver resistance of $100\ \Omega$ into node $a$ with $C_a = 10$ fF, then $200\ \Omega$ from $a$ to node $b$ with $C_b = 20$ fF. For sink $b$: $C_a$ shares only the $100\ \Omega$, and $C_b$ shares all $300\ \Omega$. So $T_b = 100 \cdot 10 + 300 \cdot 20 = 7000\ \Omega\cdot\text{fF} = 7$ ps.

## Computing it in one tree traversal

Summing over every capacitor for every sink is quadratic. A timer instead walks the tree twice. A post-order pass computes the downstream capacitance $C_{down}(v)$ of each node, the total capacitance at and below it. A pre-order pass then sets $T(v) = T(\text{parent}) + R_{edge}\, C_{down}(v)$. Each edge resistance charges everything beneath it, which is the same sum regrouped. The work is linear in the size of the net. Units matter: one ohm times one femtofarad is one femtosecond, so $1000\ \Omega\cdot\text{fF}$ is one picosecond.

label: Delay of a distributed RC wire
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Delay of a distributed RC wire

A wire is not a lumped resistor and capacitor: its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length. Modeling it as a distributed line changes the Elmore delay by a factor of two and makes delay grow with the square of length. That quadratic growth is the reason long wires need repeaters, and the reason a router's detour can wreck a path that met timing after placement.

## The distributed line halves the lumped delay

Let a wire of length $L$ have resistance $r$ per unit length and capacitance $c$ per unit length. Lumped, it would be one resistor $rL$ charging one capacitor $cL$, with time constant $rcL^2$. Split it into many small segments instead: each bit of capacitance at position $x$ sees only the resistance $rx$ between it and the driver. The Elmore sum becomes $\int_0^L r x \, c \, dx = rcL^2/2$, half the lumped value. A 350 um wire with $r = 1$ ohm/um and $c = 0.15$ fF/um gives $1 \times 0.15 \times 350^2 / 2 = 9187.5$ ohm-fF, about 9.19 ps. The same result follows from a pi model with $cL/2$ at each end.

## Driver, wire and load together

A driver of resistance $R_d$ drives the wire into a load capacitance $C_L$. The driver resistance is shared by every capacitor downstream, so it charges the whole wire plus the load, $R_d (cL + C_L)$. The wire's own resistance charges half its own capacitance, as above, plus all of the load: $rL(cL/2 + C_L)$. The total Elmore delay is $T = R_d (cL + C_L) + rL\,(cL/2 + C_L)$. For $R_d = 800$ ohm, $L = 350$ um, $r = 1$ ohm/um, $c = 0.15$ fF/um and $C_L = 20$ fF, the driver term is 58000 ohm-fF and the wire term 16187.5 ohm-fF, so the delay is about 74.19 ps. One ohm times one femtofarad is one femtosecond.

## Quadratic growth and repeaters

Only the $rcL^2/2$ term is quadratic, but for long wires it dominates. Doubling a 400 um wire to 800 um, with $R_d = 400$ ohm, $r = 2$ ohm/um, $c = 0.2$ fF/um and $C_L = 17$ fF, takes the delay from 84.4 ps to 226 ps, much more than double. Cutting the wire into $k$ segments with repeaters makes each segment's quadratic term $rc(L/k)^2/2$, so the wire part of the total falls to $rcL^2/(2k)$ at the cost of $k$ repeater delays; at the optimum the total grows linearly with length. This is why routing detours matter: a net that was estimated as a short Steiner tree at placement and routed with a long detour can gain far more delay than its extra length suggests.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter on wires; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on timing-driven routing and buffering.

label: Interpolating NLDM tables
lesson:
# Interpolating NLDM tables

Liberty's non-linear delay model stores each timing arc as small tables of delay and output slew, indexed by the input slew and the output load. A real pin almost never lands on a table point, so every delay a timer computes is an interpolation, and some are extrapolations. This lookup runs for every arc evaluation in the design, which makes it one of the hottest loops in any timer.

## Linear interpolation along one axis

A typical table has index_1 for input slew and index_2 for output load, often seven points each, with the delay at every grid point. If the query lies exactly on a grid line, for instance the slew equals an index_1 value, only the load needs interpolating: $v = v_1 + t\,(v_2 - v_1)$ with $t = (c - c_1)/(c_2 - c_1)$. Take load points 8 and 16 fF with delays 67 and 97 ps at slew 40 ps. At 14 fF, $t = 0.75$ and $v = 67 + 0.75 \times 30 = 89.5$ ps. Linear interpolation is exact for a function that is linear in load, which delay roughly is over a small window, and that is why tables need only a few points per axis.

## Bilinear interpolation in a window

In general the query falls inside a $2 \times 2$ window of slews $s_1 < s_2$ and loads $c_1 < c_2$. Interpolate along load at both slews, then along slew between the two results. In one formula,
$$v = \frac{v_{11}(s_2-s)(c_2-c) + v_{12}(s_2-s)(c-c_1) + v_{21}(s-s_1)(c_2-c) + v_{22}(s-s_1)(c-c_1)}{(s_2-s_1)(c_2-c_1)},$$
where $v_{ij}$ is the value at slew $s_i$ and load $c_j$. With $s$ at fraction $t_s$ and $c$ at fraction $t_c$, this is $(1-t_s)(1-t_c)v_{11} + (1-t_s)t_c v_{12} + t_s(1-t_c) v_{21} + t_s t_c v_{22}$. For corners 60, 68, 67 and 82 ps, $t_s = 0.75$ and $t_c = 0.375$, the result is 70.22 ps. The same lookup gives the output slew, which feeds the next stage.

## Extrapolation beyond the table

When the load or slew lies outside the table, timers such as OpenSTA extrapolate with the same formula using the nearest edge window, so a fraction greater than 1 or less than 0 appears. With load index points 1 and 2 fF and a query at 2.25 fF, $t_c = 1.25$. Extrapolation is only as good as the linear trend of the last window, and delay curves bend: a heavily loaded cell's real delay often grows faster than the edge slope predicts. Characterization ranges are chosen to cover the loads and slews the design should see, and max_capacitance and max_transition design rules keep the design inside them. A timer that silently extrapolates far beyond the table produces numbers no one characterized, so reports flag it.

## Going deeper

The Liberty reference manual on lu_table_template and NLDM; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 3; the OpenSTA source, TableModel.

label: Stage delay: cell arc plus net arc
prereqs: Delay of a distributed RC wire
RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Stage delay: cell arc plus net arc

A timing path alternates cell arcs and net arcs. A stage is one driving cell plus the net it drives up to a sink pin, and its delay is what a delay calculator computes in one call. The cell's delay depends on the load the net presents, and the net's delay depends on its own resistance and the sink pin's capacitance, so the two arcs of a stage are computed together.

## Cell delay from drive resistance and load

A simple, widely used model treats the driving cell as an intrinsic delay plus a resistor charging its load: $d_{cell} = d_0 + R_{drv} C_{load}$. The load is everything the output must charge: the wire capacitance plus every sink pin's input capacitance. With $d_0 = 20$ ps, $R_{drv} = 0.5$ kohm, a wire of 8 fF and a 4 fF sink pin, $d_{cell} = 20 + 0.5 \times 12 = 26$ ps; one kilohm times one femtofarad is one picosecond. A Liberty table refines this with slew dependence and curvature, but the linear model captures the essential trade-off: a stronger cell, smaller $R_{drv}$, is faster for the same load but presents more input capacitance to its own driver.

## Adding the net arc

The net arc runs from the driver pin to the sink pin. Model the wire as a pi network: half the wire capacitance at each end and the wire resistance $R_w$ between. The near half is charged by the driver and belongs to the cell's load; the wire resistance charges the far half plus the sink pin, so its Elmore delay is $d_{net} = R_w (C_w/2 + C_{pin})$. With $R_w = 0.3$ kohm, $C_w = 6$ fF and $C_{pin} = 1$ fF, $d_{net} = 0.3 \times 4 = 1.2$ ps. If the cell delay is 37 ps, the stage takes 38.2 ps. Short nets have tiny net delays compared with cell delays; long nets, or nets on resistive lower metal layers, do not.

## Summing stages into a path arrival

A path's arrival is its start time plus the delays of its stages in order, each stage's sink pin being the next stage's input. With a start at 30 ps and two stages of 12.45 and 22.35 ps, the arrival is 64.8 ps. Every stage couples to its neighbors. Upsizing a gate lowers its own delay but raises the load of the stage before it; a long wire raises both the driver's delay and the net delay. Delay calculation also passes slew forward: each stage's output slew becomes the next stage's input slew. That is why timers evaluate stages in level order, and why an optimizer that changes one cell must update the delays of the stage that drives it as well as its own.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapters 4 and 5; Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort" (1999), on the drive-resistance view of a gate.

label: Slew propagation: worst slew versus path slew
lesson:
# Slew propagation: worst slew versus path slew

Delay depends on input slew, so every stage's output slew must be carried to the next stage. At a pin with several inputs, the timer has to decide which slew to pass on. Graph-based timers keep one slew per pin, the worst, and that choice is the main source of graph-based pessimism that path-based analysis later removes.

## Worst-slew merging at a pin

Consider a gate G with inputs A and B. The arc from each input has its own delay and its own output slew, both functions of that input's slew. A graph-based timer stores one late arrival and one late slew at G's output, each the worst over the input arcs: the arrival is $\max(AT_A + d_A, AT_B + d_B)$ and the slew is $\max(s_{out,A}, s_{out,B})$, computed separately. With arc slews of 124 ps from A and 103 ps from B, the timer stores 124 ps, even if the latest arrival came from B. The stored pair may not belong to any single real transition, but it bounds them all, because larger slews only increase downstream delays. OpenSTA follows this rule by default.

## Downstream arrival under graph-based analysis

The next gate H computes its delay from the merged slew. If H's arc delay is $a_H + k_H s$, the arrival at H's output is $AT_G + a_H + k_H \max(s_{out})$. For a G output arrival of 162 ps, a merged slew of 87 ps and $d_H = 36 + 0.3 s$, the arrival at H is $162 + 36 + 26.1 = 224.1$ ps. The latest arrival came through input A with a slew of 81 ps, but H was timed with B's 87 ps slew. Every downstream stage inherits the pessimism, and on deep paths through many merges it accumulates. A late slew that stems from a short, non-critical side input can inflate the delay of the critical path by several picoseconds.

## Path-based re-timing removes the pessimism

Path-based analysis re-times one specific path with the slews that actually travel along it. For the path through A, H's delay uses A's own output slew of 81 ps instead of 87 ps: $36 + 0.3 \times 81 = 60.3$ ps rather than 62.1 ps, so the arrival drops by 1.8 ps. In general the pessimism removed at one merge is $k_H (s_{max} - s_{path})$. Because PBA uses the real slew of the path being reported, its slack is always at least the GBA slack for that path. It is also much more expensive: it works one path at a time and cannot be updated in bulk, so tools use GBA for optimization and PBA to recover pessimism on the worst paths before signoff.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter on path-based analysis; the OpenSTA documentation on slew propagation.

label: Effective capacitance of a resistive load
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Effective capacitance of a resistive load

Liberty tables assume a cell drives a pure capacitor. A real routed net has resistance between the driver and the far capacitance, which shields part of it: during the fast output transition the driver does not see the full load. Effective capacitance is the single capacitance that makes the table give the right answer for the real resistive load. Every modern delay calculator computes it, iterating because the answer depends on the driver's own transition.

## Resistive shielding

Reduce the net to a pi model: $C_1$ at the driver pin, a resistance $R$, and $C_2$ at the far end. The far capacitor charges through $R$ with time constant $\tau = R C_2$. If the driver's output ramp is fast compared with $\tau$, the far capacitor barely charges during the ramp, and the driver sees mostly $C_1$. If the ramp is slow, the far capacitor keeps up and the driver sees nearly $C_1 + C_2$. With $R = 650$ ohm and $C_2 = 33$ fF, $\tau = 21450$ ohm-fF, or 21.45 ps. Using the total capacitance in the table would overestimate the delay at the driver pin, sometimes by a large margin on long resistive nets.

## Charge matching over a ramp

Model the driver as a ramp of duration $T$ at its pin. The near capacitor takes its full charge; the far capacitor, driven through $R$, reaches only the fraction $1 - (\tau/T)(1 - e^{-T/\tau})$ of the swing by the end of the ramp. Matching the total charge gives
$$C_{eff} = C_1 + C_2\left[1 - \frac{\tau}{T}\left(1 - e^{-T/\tau}\right)\right].$$
For $C_1 = 25$ fF, $C_2 = 54$ fF, $\tau = 21.6$ ps and $T = 171$ ps, $\tau/T = 0.1263$ and the far capacitor contributes 47.18 fF, so $C_{eff} = 72.18$ fF against a total of 79 fF. As $T/\tau$ grows, the bracket tends to 1 and $C_{eff}$ to the total; as it shrinks, $C_{eff}$ tends to $C_1$.

## Iterating with the cell table

The ramp time itself comes from the cell's table, evaluated at the load, which is $C_{eff}$: a fixed-point problem. Start from the total capacitance, look up the ramp time, compute a new $C_{eff}$, and repeat until the two agree. With a ramp time of $7 + 2C$ ps, starting at $C_{tot} = 37$ fF gives $T = 81$ ps, and with $\tau = 7.8$ ps the first update is $C_{eff} = 35.84$ fF. Since $C_{eff} \le C_{tot}$, the next ramp is shorter, which lowers $C_{eff}$ slightly again; a few iterations converge. Calculators in OpenSTA such as the dmp_ceff family fit a driver model to the table and refine this idea, and the waveform at the far end is then computed from the RC network rather than from the table.

## Going deeper

Qian, Pullela and Pillage, "Modeling the effective capacitance for the RC interconnect of CMOS gates" (IEEE TCAD, 1994); Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 5.

label: Setup and hold checks
lesson:
# Setup and hold checks

Every flop-to-flop path is checked twice. The setup check asks whether the slowest data reaches the capture flop before the next capturing edge; the hold check asks whether the fastest data stays away long enough not to corrupt the value being captured on the current edge. Both use the same arrival and clock numbers, combined in opposite directions, and a timer reports each as a slack.

## The setup required time

Data launched by the edge at 0 must be captured by the next edge, one period $T$ later. The capture flop's clock pin sees that edge after its clock latency $L_{cap}$, and the data must be stable a setup time $t_{su}$ before it. The setup required time at the D pin is therefore $RAT = T + L_{cap} - t_{su}$. For an 800 ps period, a capture latency of 185 ps and a 29 ps setup time, data must arrive by $800 + 185 - 29 = 956$ ps. Clock uncertainty, when specified, is subtracted too. The launch side contributes nothing to the required time: it determines the arrival, not the deadline.

## Setup slack

The latest arrival at the D pin is the launch clock latency plus clock-to-Q plus the longest combinational delay: $AT = L_{launch} + t_{cq} + d_{max}$. Setup slack is the required time minus this arrival:
$$S_{setup} = (T + L_{cap} - t_{su}) - (L_{launch} + t_{cq} + d_{max}).$$
With $T = 1100$, $L_{cap} = 170$, $t_{su} = 36$, $L_{launch} = 140$, $t_{cq} = 74$ and $d_{max} = 410$ ps, the slack is $1234 - 624 = 610$ ps. The difference $L_{cap} - L_{launch}$ is the clock skew; positive skew adds setup margin. Setup failures are fixed by making the long path faster, lengthening the period, or shifting the clock edges.

## Hold slack

Hold compares the same capturing edge that the data was launched with. New data launched at time 0 must not reach the capture flop before the flop has held its old value for the hold time after its own clock arrival:
$$S_{hold} = (L_{launch} + t_{cq} + d_{min}) - (L_{cap} + t_h).$$
With $L_{launch} = 135$, $t_{cq} = 61$, $d_{min} = 26$, $L_{cap} = 125$ and $t_h = 28$ ps, the slack is $222 - 153 = 69$ ps. The period $T$ does not appear, so slowing the clock never fixes hold. Hold uses the shortest path and minimum delays, usually at the fast corner, and positive skew hurts it. The fix is to add delay to the short path, which is why hold fixing comes after setup fixing.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 8; Harris and Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture", the section on timing of sequential logic.

label: Minimum clock period of a register path
lesson:
# Minimum clock period of a register path

The setup check can be turned around: instead of asking whether a path meets a given period, ask for the smallest period it meets. That number, and its inverse, the maximum frequency, is how architects and implementation teams talk about a design, and it shows directly which path limits the clock.

## The smallest period one path meets

Set the setup slack to zero and solve for $T$. With skew defined as capture latency minus launch latency, setup holds when
$$T \ge t_{cq} + d_{max} + t_{su} - \text{skew}.$$
For $t_{cq} = 50$ ps, $d_{max} = 550$ ps, $t_{su} = 60$ ps and a skew of -15 ps, the path needs $50 + 550 + 60 + 15 = 675$ ps. Negative skew, a capture clock that arrives early, raises the required period; positive skew lowers it, which is the basis of useful skew. Clock uncertainty adds directly to the bound. Each term names a lever: a faster flop, faster logic, a smaller setup time, or a later capture clock.

## The design's minimum period

A design meets a period only if every register path does, so its minimum period is the largest per-path minimum: $T_{min} = \max_p (t_{cq} + d_p + t_{su} - \text{skew}_p)$. With two paths needing 887 ps and 676 ps, the design needs 887 ps. The limiting path is the critical path, and its slack at any period $T$ equals $T - T_{min}$. Two paths with similar logic delay can rank differently once skew is counted: a path whose capture clock is late can tolerate more logic. Pipelining raises frequency by cutting the worst path's logic delay, at the cost of extra flop overhead $t_{cq} + t_{su}$ in each new stage, which limits how far it pays.

## Converting to frequency

Frequency is the inverse of the period. With the period in picoseconds, $f_{max} = 10^6 / T_{min}$ MHz, because one MHz has a period of $10^6$ ps. A minimum period of 981 ps gives about 1019.4 MHz; 1250 ps gives 800 MHz. Frequency is not linear in delay: shaving 50 ps off a 1000 ps path gains about 52.6 MHz, while the same 50 ps off a 500 ps path gains about 222 MHz. When teams quote a target frequency, the timer turns it into a period with create_clock, and all checks work in time. Reporting the margin as slack in ps rather than as MHz keeps different paths comparable.

## Going deeper

Harris and Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture", the section on timing of sequential logic; Hennessy and Patterson on pipelining overhead.

label: Half-cycle paths between opposite edges
lesson:
# Half-cycle paths between opposite edges

Not every path runs between rising edges. A path from a rising-edge flop to a falling-edge flop, or the reverse, has only part of a cycle for setup, and an unusually easy hold check. Such half-cycle paths appear in DDR interfaces, in negative-edge logic and around latches, and a timer derives their checks from the clock waveform rather than from the period alone.

## Time between launch and capture edges

Let a clock rise at 0 and fall at $H$, with period $T$. For a rise-launch, fall-capture path, the setup capture edge is the first falling edge after launch, at $H$: the path has $H$ instead of $T$. For a fall-launch, rise-capture path, data leaves at $H$ and is captured by the rising edge at $T$, a window of $T - H$. With a 50 percent duty cycle both are $T/2$. With $T = 1600$ ps and $H = 784$ ps, a fall-to-rise path gets 816 ps. Any duty-cycle distortion in the clock tree directly shrinks one of these windows, so half-cycle paths are sensitive to clock waveform quality.

## Setup slack of a half-cycle path

The check is the usual setup check with the shorter window: $S = W - t_{su} - (t_{cq} + d_{max})$, where $W$ is the launch-to-capture window. With $W = 600$ ps, $t_{su} = 47$, $t_{cq} = 50$ and $d_{max} = 240$ ps, the slack is 263 ps. The same logic between two rising-edge flops would have had 600 ps more. Half-cycle paths therefore carry less logic, and a designer who moves a flop to the opposite edge to fix hold or to retime a signal must check that the remaining logic fits the half cycle. Clock latencies and uncertainty enter exactly as in a full-cycle check.

## Hold is easy for half-cycle paths

Hold is checked against the capturing edge just before the setup capture edge. For rise-to-fall that is the falling edge at $H - T$, before the launch at 0. The hold slack is $(t_{cq} + d_{min}) - ((H - T) + t_h)$, which is large: with $T = 1300$, $H = 585$, $t_{cq} = 63$, $d_{min} = 35$ and $t_h = 28$ ps, it is $98 - (-715 + 28) = 785$ ps. For fall-to-rise, the hold edge is the rise at 0, $H$ before the launch. This is why designers sometimes insert a negative-edge flop or latch to repair hold on paths with large clock skew: the half-cycle offset turns a hold problem into a setup budget.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 8 on half-cycle paths.

label: Recovery and removal checks
lesson:
# Recovery and removal checks

Asynchronous set and reset pins act immediately, without the clock, but releasing them is not instantaneous in effect: if a reset deasserts too close to a clock edge, the flop may not leave reset cleanly on that edge, and different flops may leave reset on different cycles. Recovery and removal are the setup and hold checks for the deasserting edge of an asynchronous control.

## The recovery required time

Recovery is the setup-like check. The deassertion must reach the asynchronous pin at least the recovery time $t_{rec}$ before the active clock edge at that flop. With a reset synchronized and launched by one clock edge, the next capturing edge arrives at $T + L_{cap}$, so the required time is $T + L_{cap} - t_{rec}$. For a 1000 ps clock, a capture latency of 110 ps and a 73 ps recovery time, the deassertion must arrive by 1037 ps. Liberty models these checks as timing arcs from the clock pin to the reset pin, with timing types recovery_rising and removal_rising, characterized like setup and hold.

## Recovery slack

The deassertion arrives at $L_{launch} + t_{cq} + d_{max}$, where $d_{max}$ is the longest path of the reset net, often a large buffered tree reaching thousands of flops. Recovery slack is required minus arrival. With a required time of 1127 ps and an arrival of $60 + 44 + 680 = 784$ ps, the slack is 343 ps. Large reset trees make recovery a real constraint: the reset fan-out can rival a clock tree in size, but it is buffered as data. If recovery fails, flops leave reset on different cycles, and a state machine can start in an illegal state. Designs therefore deassert reset synchronously through a reset synchronizer and time the tree like any data path.

## Removal slack

Removal is the hold-like check. The deassertion must not arrive so soon after the clock edge that it falls inside the removal window: $S_{rem} = (L_{launch} + t_{cq} + d_{min}) - (L_{cap} + t_{rem})$. With $140 + 79 + 85 = 304$ ps against $120 + 52 = 172$ ps, the slack is 132 ps. As with hold, the period does not appear. Only deassertion is checked. Assertion takes effect asynchronously regardless of the clock, so a timer has nothing to compare it against; whatever logic consumes the reset must tolerate its asynchronous arrival. Recovery and removal appear in reports alongside setup and hold, in their own path groups.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 8 on recovery and removal; Cummings and Mills, "Synchronous Resets? Asynchronous Resets? I am so confused!" (SNUG 2002).

label: Latches and time borrowing
lesson:
# Latches and time borrowing

A level-sensitive latch is transparent while its clock is active, so data may arrive after the latch opens and still pass through. A path that arrives late at a latch borrows time from the next stage. Timers must model this to avoid reporting false violations on latch-based designs, and they must charge the borrowed time to the following path so that nothing is counted twice.

## Borrowing past the opening edge

Take a positive latch clocked with period $T$ and a 50 percent duty cycle, fed by a rising-edge flop that launches at 0. The latch's nominal capture point is its opening edge at $T$. If data arrives at $A \le T$, it waits for the latch to open: no borrowing. If it arrives later, while the latch is transparent, it passes straight through and the path borrows $A - T$. With $T = 1100$ ps and $A = 1550$ ps, the borrow is 450 ps. To the path ending at the latch the borrowing is not a violation; reports show it as time borrowed with zero slack, as long as the arrival stays within the borrowing limit.

## The maximum borrow

Data must still settle a setup time before the latch closes, at $T + H$ where $H$ is the high time. The latest legal arrival is $T + H - t_{su}$, so the most a path can borrow is the pulse width minus setup, $H - t_{su}$. With $H = 700$ ps and $t_{su} = 38$ ps, the limit is 662 ps. Beyond it the path truly fails setup at the closing edge. Timers allow the limit to be reduced, for example with set_max_time_borrow, so that a designer can keep borrowing within a budget. Clock skew and uncertainty at the latch adjust the opening and closing edges just as they adjust a flop's capture edge.

## Charging the next stage

Borrowed time is taken from the path that starts at the latch. When borrowing, data leaves the latch at $A + d_{DQ}$, the arrival plus the latch's D-to-Q delay, rather than at the opening edge plus clock-to-Q. The next path is timed from there. If the latch's output feeds 220 ps of logic to a flop capturing at $2T = 2000$ ps with a 50 ps setup, and $A = 1200$, $d_{DQ} = 60$ ps, the next stage's slack is $2000 - 50 - (1200 + 60 + 220) = 470$ ps. Borrowing passes slack along a pipeline: a long stage can take time from a short neighbor. A timer must propagate this across chains of latches, which makes latch-based timing iterative rather than a single pass.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 8 on time borrowing; Sakallah, Mudge and Olukotun, "Analysis and design of latch-controlled synchronous digital circuits" (DAC 1990).

label: Choosing the right timing check
lesson:
# Choosing the right timing check

A timer applies different checks at different pins: setup and hold at flop data pins, recovery and removal at asynchronous controls, clock-gating checks at gates that combine a clock with an enable, minimum pulse width at clock pins, and data-to-data checks where two signals must stay aligned. A tool designer must know which check each structure needs, because a missing check is a silent hole in signoff.

## Data and asynchronous checks

Setup guards against data that arrives too late for the next capturing edge; hold guards against new data that arrives too early and corrupts the current capture. Both are checked at the data pins of flip-flops and latches against the clock pin, using Liberty check arcs. For asynchronous set and reset, the deasserting edge is checked against the clock with recovery, the setup-like check, and removal, the hold-like check. Assertion is not checked because it acts without the clock. For a latch, setup is checked against the closing edge with borrowing allowed after the opening edge. Each check type has its own path group in reports, so a design can pass setup while failing recovery.

## Clock-pin and gating checks

When a gate such as an AND combines a clock with an enable, the enable must change only while the clock is in its controlling state, low for an AND, or the gated clock glitches. Timers infer clock-gating setup and hold checks on the enable pin, or apply them from integrated clock-gating cells in the library. Clock pins also need a minimum pulse width: unequal rise and fall delays along a long clock tree, or a divider, can shrink the high or low phase below what the flop needs to latch reliably. Liberty gives the limit, and the timer checks the propagated pulse. A data-to-data check, set with set_data_check, times one data pin against another when two signals must arrive within a window and neither is a clock.

## Matching checks to failures

The right fix depends on which check failed. A hold failure needs delay added on the short path, sized at the fast corner and limited by setup slack at the slow corner; changing the period does nothing. A path between opposite clock edges gets a partial cycle for setup and an easy hold check. An input from an unrelated clock domain has no defined launch-capture relationship at all: no setup or hold check is meaningful, so the crossing is declared asynchronous and handled by a synchronizer. When reading a report, first identify the check type and its capture edge; many apparent violations come from checks applied with the wrong edge relationship.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 8; the Liberty reference manual on timing_type values.

D) Setup on the D pin

problems.e: Deassertion of an asynchronous control is timed against the clock: recovery is the setup-like check and removal the hold-like one.

label: Clock waveforms and create_clock
lesson:
# Clock waveforms and create_clock

Every check in a timer is measured against clock edges, and those edges come from the clock definitions in SDC. create_clock gives a clock a name, a source, a period and a waveform, the times of its rising and falling edges within one period. Reading a waveform correctly, and knowing where each edge falls in later cycles, is the first step in deriving any launch and capture relationship.

## Period and duty cycle

The command create_clock -name clk -period 10 -waveform {0 5} [get_ports clk] defines a clock on port clk with period 10 time units, rising at 0 and falling at 5. The waveform lists edge times in increasing order within the first period, first a rise and then a fall; without -waveform the default is a rise at 0 and a fall at half the period. The duty cycle is the fraction of the period the clock is high, $(t_{fall} - t_{rise}) / P$. For -period 13 -waveform {6 8} the clock is high for 2 of every 13 units, about 15.4 percent. Units are those of the library or the session, usually ns.

## Edges in later cycles

The waveform repeats every period: rising edges occur at $t_{rise} + kP$ and falling edges at $t_{fall} + kP$ for integers $k$. Counting the rise at $t_{rise}$ as the first, rising edge number $n$ is at $t_{rise} + (n-1)P$. For -period 17 -waveform {4 16}, the fourth rising edge is at $4 + 3 \times 17 = 55$. A timer enumerates edges this way when it pairs launch and capture edges, especially between clocks with different periods, where the pattern repeats only after the least common multiple of the periods. The clock's source latency and network latency then shift each edge as seen at a particular flop.

## Finding the next edge after a time

Many questions reduce to finding the first edge of a given kind after some time $t_0$: the capture edge for a launch, the closing edge of a latch, or the edge a generated clock follows. For falling edges, take the smallest $k$ with $t_{fall} + kP > t_0$. For -period 14 -waveform {0 2} and $t_0 = 19$, the falling edges are at 2, 16, 30, so the answer is 30. Whether the edge must be strictly later or may coincide matters: a setup check pairs a launch with a strictly later capture edge, while a hold check uses the edge that coincides with or precedes it. Writing the inequality explicitly avoids an off-by-one-cycle error, the most common bug in hand edge arithmetic.

## Going deeper

The Synopsys Design Constraints format specification, create_clock; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 7.

label: Clock source and network latency
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Clock source and network latency

A clock edge does not reach every flop at the same time. It first travels from its true origin, an oscillator or PLL, to the point where the clock is defined, and then through the on-chip clock tree to each sink. These two delays, source latency and network latency, decide when each flop actually launches and captures, and their difference between two flops is skew.

## Clock arrival at a sink

Source latency is the delay from the clock's origin to its definition point, set in SDC with set_clock_latency -source. Network latency is the delay from the definition point through the clock buffers and wires to a flop's clock pin. With propagated clocks, the timer computes it from the actual tree; with ideal clocks, it uses a value from set_clock_latency. The clock arrival at a sink is the sum. For a source latency of 70 ps, shared buffers of 37 and 29 ps and branch buffers of 29 and 32 ps, the edge launched at 0 reaches the flop at $70 + 37 + 29 + 29 + 32 = 197$ ps. In OpenSTA, clocks stay ideal until set_propagated_clock is applied.

## Skew between two sinks

Skew is the capture clock arrival minus the launch clock arrival. The source latency and any shared trunk of the tree appear in both, so they cancel: only the branches after the split point matter. If the launch branch adds 48 ps after the split and the capture branch 36 ps, the skew is -12 ps, whatever the source latency and trunk delays. This is why clock tree synthesis tries to balance branch delays, and why the location of the split point matters for variation: a long shared trunk is harmless for skew, and later the common path is also credited back by clock reconvergence pessimism removal.

## Propagated clocks in the setup check

With propagated clocks, the setup check uses each flop's actual clock arrival: $S = T + L_{cap} - t_{su} - (L_{launch} + t_{cq} + d)$. With a 600 ps period, launch and capture arrivals of 126 and 145 ps, $t_{cq} = 53$, $d = 470$ and $t_{su} = 37$ ps, the slack is 59 ps. Before clock tree synthesis there is no tree to propagate through: the clock net is a single huge unbuffered net, so timers use ideal clocks with an estimated latency and add a skew budget to clock uncertainty. After synthesis the clocks are switched to propagated, and the skew budget is dropped from the uncertainty, so that skew is not counted twice.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 7 on clock latency; the OpenSTA documentation for set_propagated_clock.

label: Clock skew and jitter
lesson:
# Clock skew and jitter

Two effects move clock edges away from their ideal times: skew, a fixed spatial difference in arrival between two flops, and jitter, a random temporal variation of the edges themselves. They enter the setup and hold checks differently, and confusing them, or counting either twice, is a classic source of wrong slack.

## Signed skew

Skew is the capture clock arrival minus the launch clock arrival, $\text{skew} = L_{cap} - L_{launch}$. It is signed. With a launch arrival of 190 ps and a capture arrival of 85 ps, the skew is -105 ps: the capture flop sees the edge early. Positive skew gives the data more time for setup and less margin for hold; negative skew does the reverse. Skew is a property of a launch and capture pair, not of a single flop, so one flop can have positive skew with respect to one neighbor and negative skew with respect to another. Global skew, the largest difference across all sinks, is a tree-quality metric but does not enter any single check.

## Setup slack with skew and jitter

Cycle-to-cycle jitter is the variation of one clock period relative to the previous one. A setup check spans one cycle, from a launch edge to the next capture edge, so jitter $J$ can shorten that cycle and is subtracted:
$$S_{setup} = T - J + \text{skew} - t_{su} - t_{cq} - d_{max}.$$
With $T = 800$, $J = 37$, skew -35, $t_{su} = 53$, $t_{cq} = 46$ and $d_{max} = 260$ ps, the slack is 369 ps. In SDC, jitter is usually folded into set_clock_uncertainty rather than modeled separately, together with a margin and, before CTS, an estimate of skew.

## Hold slack with skew

Hold compares launch and capture on the same edge, so the period and the cycle-to-cycle jitter between consecutive edges do not enter it:
$$S_{hold} = t_{cq} + d_{min} - t_h - \text{skew}.$$
With $t_{cq} = 79$, $d_{min} = 75$, $t_h = 33$ and a skew of -15 ps, the slack is 136 ps. Positive skew subtracts directly from hold slack, which is why flops with short paths between them, such as shift registers, are sensitive to skew: a capture clock that arrives late lets the new data race through. Hold uncertainty in SDC adds margin for effects such as the jitter of a single edge seen differently at two sinks.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 7; Friedman, "Clock distribution networks in synchronous digital integrated circuits" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2001).

label: Clock uncertainty in setup and hold
lesson:
# Clock uncertainty in setup and hold

set_clock_uncertainty is the SDC knob that reserves margin on clock edges. Setup uncertainty makes the capturing edge effectively earlier; hold uncertainty makes the hold requirement larger. What the number should contain changes during the flow: before clock tree synthesis it stands in for skew that does not exist yet, and after it only jitter and margin remain.

## Building a pre-CTS uncertainty

Before CTS, clocks are ideal and every flop sees the same edge, so the timer knows nothing about skew. Teams therefore budget setup uncertainty as the sum of the expected jitter, an estimate of the skew the tree will add, and a design margin. With 10 ps of jitter, an 85 ps skew estimate and 15 ps of margin, the command is set_clock_uncertainty -setup 110 [get_clocks clk]. After CTS, clocks become propagated and the timer computes real skew, so the skew estimate must be removed from the uncertainty; leaving it in counts skew twice and makes the design look worse than it is. Uncertainty can also be set between specific clock pairs, for crossings with extra jitter.

## Setup slack with uncertainty

Setup uncertainty $U_s$ is subtracted from the required time: $S = T - U_s - t_{su} - (t_{cq} + d_{max})$ with ideal clocks. For $T = 700$, $U_s = 41$, $t_{su} = 39$, $t_{cq} = 43$ and $d_{max} = 310$ ps, the slack is 267 ps. Path reports list the uncertainty as its own line in the required-time section, so it can be audited. Because it applies to every path of a clock, a too-large uncertainty is an expensive mistake: it makes the optimizer upsize and buffer thousands of paths that would have passed, costing area and power.

## Hold slack with uncertainty

Hold uncertainty $U_h$ is added to the hold requirement: $S = (t_{cq} + d_{min}) - (t_h + U_h)$ with ideal clocks. For $t_{cq} = 30$, $d_{min} = 99$, $t_h = 42$ and $U_h = 13$ ps, the slack is 74 ps. Hold uncertainty is usually smaller than setup uncertainty, because cycle-to-cycle jitter does not apply to a same-edge check; what remains covers the uncertainty of one edge at two sinks and modeling error. Pre-CTS, a hold skew budget is sometimes included, but hold fixing is generally postponed until after CTS, when real skew is known, so buffers are not inserted against skew that never materializes.

## Going deeper

The Synopsys Design Constraints format specification, set_clock_uncertainty; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 7.

label: Generated clocks
lesson:
# Generated clocks

Many clocks on a chip are derived from others: divided by a counter, multiplied by a PLL, or shaped by selecting particular master edges. SDC describes them with create_generated_clock, which ties the new clock to a master. That tie lets the timer compute the generated clock's edges and its latency through the generating logic, so paths between master and generated domains are timed with the correct relationship.

## Dividing a master clock

create_generated_clock -name div2 -source [get_ports clk] -divide_by 2 [get_pins U1/Q] declares that the clock at the divider flop's output has twice the master's period. In general -divide_by $N$ gives period $N T$ and -multiply_by $M$ gives $T/M$. A 4 ns master divided by 8 is a 32 ns clock. Defining the divider output with a separate create_clock instead would create an unrelated clock: paths between clk and the divided domain would lose their phase relationship, and the latency through the divider would not be computed. The generated clock's edges are aligned to the master edges that produce them, which create_generated_clock derives automatically.

## Building a waveform from master edges

The -edges option builds the generated waveform from numbered master edges: edge 1 is the master's first rise, edge 2 its first fall, edge 3 its second rise, and so on. A list {e1 e2 e3} means the generated clock rises at master edge e1, falls at e2 and rises again at e3. For a 4 ns master with waveform {0 2}, edges are at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Then -edges {1 4 7} rises at 0, falls at 6 and rises at 12: period 12 ns, high for 6 ns, a divide-by-3 with 50 percent duty cycle. The high time is $t(e_2) - t(e_1)$ and the period $t(e_3) - t(e_1)$. -edge_shift can offset each edge further.

## Latency through the generating logic

With propagated clocks, a generated clock's source latency is the master's source latency plus the delay from the master's definition point through its network to the divider and through the divider itself. A sink in the generated domain then adds the generated clock's own network. With a master source latency of 200 ps, 380 ps of master network to the divider flop, a 68 ps clock-to-Q and 390 ps of generated network, the edge reaches the sink at 1038 ps. If a master-domain flop near the divider sees its clock at about 580 ps, a path from it to that sink has about 458 ps of skew, which the timer computes only because the generated clock was declared relative to its master.

## Going deeper

The Synopsys Design Constraints format specification, create_generated_clock; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 7.

label: Setup and hold relationships between clocks
lesson:
# Setup and hold relationships between clocks

When launch and capture flops are clocked by different but synchronous clocks, there is no single period to plug into the setup check. The timer must find, among all pairs of launch and capture edges, the most restrictive pair for setup, and then derive the hold check from it. This edge arithmetic underlies every multi-frequency path and every multicycle exception.

## Integer-multiple periods

Take two clocks from one source, both rising at 0. For each launch edge, the setup capture edge is the nearest capture edge strictly later. If the launch clock has period 4 ns and the capture clock 16 ns, the launch edges at 0, 4, 8 and 12 all pair with the capture edge at 16, with gaps of 16, 12, 8 and 4. The most restrictive setup relationship is 4 ns, from the last launch edge before capture. From slow to fast, launch at 16 ns and capture at 4 ns, the launch at 0 pairs with the capture at 4, and the setup relationship is 4 ns. In both directions the faster clock's period sets the setup relationship unless a multicycle exception says the design waits longer.

## General periods over the common period

For periods that are not multiples, the edge pattern repeats after the least common multiple. With launch period 9 ns and capture 6 ns, the common period is 18 ns, and the launch edges at 0 and 9 pair with capture edges at 6 and 12: gaps of 6 and 3, so the setup relationship is 3 ns. With periods 10 and 4 the common period is 20 ns, launches at 0 and 10 pair with 4 and 12, and the relationship is 2 ns. Clocks whose periods have no small common multiple produce tiny, unrealistic relationships; that usually means they should be declared asynchronous rather than timed.

## Deriving the hold relationship

Hold is derived from the most restrictive setup pair, launch at $t$ and capture at $c$. Two checks follow. Data launched at $t$ must not be captured by the capture edge one period before, at $c - T_c$, giving $(c - T_c) - t$. Data launched by the next launch edge, at $t + T_l$, must not be captured by $c$, giving $c - (t + T_l)$. The larger of the two is the hold relationship. For launch period 3 and capture period 8, the tightest setup pair is launch at 15 and capture at 16; the two values are $8 - 15 = -7$ and $16 - 18 = -2$, so hold is checked with -2 ns. For equal periods both values are 0, the familiar same-edge hold.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 8 on multi-frequency paths; the PrimeTime and OpenSTA documentation on clock relationships.

label: Clock reconvergence pessimism removal
lesson:
# Clock reconvergence pessimism removal

Under on-chip variation, a timer takes the launch clock path late and the capture clock path early for setup. But the two paths usually share a trunk from the clock root to a branch point, and a physical buffer cannot be slow and fast at the same moment. Clock reconvergence pessimism removal, CPPR or CRPR, adds back the difference on that shared segment.

## The common point and its arrivals

Trace the launch and capture clock paths from the root. They share buffers until the branch point where they split; this last shared pin is the common point. With min and max delays per buffer, the common segment has an early arrival, the sum of its early delays, and a late arrival, the sum of its late delays. For buffers of 38/46, 37/49 and 34/41 ps (early/late), the common point arrives at 109 ps early and 136 ps late. The setup check uses 136 ps on the launch side and 109 ps on the capture side, although the real edge reaches the common point only once.

## The pessimism credit

The double counting equals the late arrival minus the early arrival at the common point: credit $= \sum_{\text{common}} (d_{late} - d_{early})$. For the segment above it is $136 - 109 = 27$ ps. With a single shared buffer of 49/60 ps, the credit is 11 ps. Only the common segment counts; the branches after the split can genuinely differ, because they are different buffers that may vary independently. A timer computes the credit per path by finding the common point of its launch and capture clocks. For hold, launch is taken early and capture late; the shared segment again cannot be both, so the same credit is added to the hold slack.

## Slack after CPPR

The corrected slack is the raw slack plus the credit. For a 1000 ps period, a launch clock of 173 ps late, a capture clock of 168 ps early, clock-to-Q 43 ps, data 470 ps and setup 30 ps, the raw slack is $1000 + 168 - 30 - 686 = 452$ ps, and adding the 27 ps credit gives 479 ps. Reports show the credit as a clock reconvergence pessimism line in the required-time section. CPPR matters most for paths whose flops share a long tree, which is most local paths, and for hold checks between nearby flops. It also matters in multi-cycle and generated-clock paths, where the common path can include the generating logic. Without it, OCV derating would be prohibitively pessimistic.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 10 on on-chip variation and CRPR; the OpenSTA documentation on CRPR.

label: SDC timing constraints
prereqs: Clock uncertainty in setup and hold
lesson:
# SDC timing constraints

A timer knows nothing about intent until it reads constraints. The Synopsys Design Constraints format, SDC, is a set of Tcl commands that define clocks, the environment at the block boundary, and the exceptions to single-cycle timing. Every slack in a report is only as correct as the SDC behind it, and constraint bugs are among the most common causes of silicon timing failures.

## Defining clocks

create_clock names a clock, its source port or pin, its period and its waveform. create_generated_clock derives a clock from a master, by -divide_by, -multiply_by or -edges, and keeps the phase relationship so paths between the two domains are timed correctly. set_clock_latency gives latency: -source for the delay from the clock's origin to its definition point, and without -source an ideal network latency used before clock tree synthesis. set_propagated_clock tells the timer to compute network latency from the built tree instead. set_clock_uncertainty reserves margin for jitter and, before CTS, expected skew, with separate -setup and -hold values. Declaring a divided clock as an independent create_clock is a typical mistake: it severs the relationship to the master.

## Constraining the block boundary

Inside a block the timer sees flops; at its ports it needs a model of the outside. set_input_delay gives the arrival at an input port relative to a clock edge, standing in for an external launch flop and its logic. set_output_delay gives how much of the cycle the logic and setup outside the block consume after an output port, so the port's required time is the capture edge minus that value. set_driving_cell or set_input_transition gives input ports a realistic slew, and set_load adds the capacitance an output port drives. An input port with no input delay is unconstrained: its paths are never reported, which is why constraint checks flag missing I/O constraints.

## Object queries and units

SDC commands apply to design objects found with get_ports, get_pins, get_cells, get_nets and get_clocks. The query matters because one name can denote different objects, and a query that matches nothing makes the constraint silently disappear. SDC numbers carry no units: the timer interprets them in the time unit of the library or session, usually ns, so a team that writes 200 meaning ps against an ns library sets a 200 ns constraint. Robust flows check that every clock reaches its sinks, every port is constrained and every exception matches something, using reports such as check_timing. In OpenSTA, read_sdc applies the file after the design is linked, so the objects it names must exist.

## Going deeper

The Synopsys Design Constraints format specification; Gangadharan and Churiwala, "Constraining Designs for Synthesis and Timing Analysis: A Practical Guide to Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)" (2013).

problems.q:
A divide-by-2 flop's output clocks half the design. How should it be constrained?

A) A second create_clock with twice the period on the divider output

B) set_clock_latency equal to the divider delay

C) create_generated_clock on the divider output with -source and -divide_by 2

D) set_multicycle_path 2 on every path it clocks
problems.a: create_generated_clock on the divider output with -source and -divide_by 2
problems.e: A generated clock keeps its phase relationship to the master and lets the timer include the path through the divider in its latency. An independent create_clock would lose that relationship.

D) din is a false path for 300 units
